Seminar Title:

Heatwaves and Urban Thermal Resilience in India: Characterization, Modelling, and Mitigation Strategies

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Speaker Name:

Lakshman Kesireddy ( Rollno : 521er1006)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Room No: 304, ER Dept

Date and Time:

04 Aug 2026 11:00 AM

Contact:

Krishna Kishore Osuri

Abstract:

Heatwaves are a major environmental and societal concern, as they directly affect human health, agriculture, the economy, and other sectors. Understanding and predicting heatwave characteristics in India remains a challenge due to a lack of high-resolution observations and coarse-resolution reanalysis, which limit analysis at the regional and urban scales. The presented thesis aims to understand the characterization of heatwaves and urban thermal resilience in India using observations, reanalysis, and modelling approaches, and has been addressed in four working chapters.&nbspThe first chapter presents the introduction, literature survey, and research objectives. &nbspChapter 2 highlights the characteristics of heatwaves that IMDAA exhibited a total of 202 heatwave days in north central India (NCI) and 181 days in the southeast coast of India (SECI) regions, while ERA5 underestimated to 132 (89) days, respectively, compared with those of IMD (195 and 163 days). The average length of the heatwave is 7.8, 7.5, and 7.76 days (8.15, 7.72, and 6.1 days) over NCI (SECI) in IMD, IMDAA, and ERA5, respectively.&nbsp The heat dome structure with a Tmax anomaly of &gt4&degC is evident up to the 850 hPa level in both analyses. Chapter 3 demonstrates that the frequency and duration of far-future heatwaves are projected to increase by ~5 events and &sim20 days per season at 95% confidence. The Western Himalayas are projected to become an emerging heatwave hotspot from the near future onwards, and the Northeast and Interior Peninsular regions in the far future. Further, the Northeast, Western Himalaya, and Northwest regions are sensitive to population, climate, and interaction effects on population exposure.&nbsp The fourth chapter reveals that heatwaves are realistically simulated in NOAH LSM with less bias in Tmax (-2 to 2&degC) up to day-5 simulation compared to SLAB and RUC (more than -5&degC). The SM in NOAH (~0.15 m3m-3) is comparable to that of the ESA CCI satellite and, hence, yields better heatwave simulation in NOAH than in the other runs. Sensitive studies highlighted the importance of vegetation in reducing heatwave days and intensity, urban physics with more realistic urban representation (horizontal extent and building heights) for improved heatwave simulation. The fifth chapter reveals that the Cool Roof (albedo 0.8) exhibited higher reductions of ~0.6&degC, ~0.5&degC, and ~0.4&degC in T2, HI, and Urban Heat Island (UHI), respectively, compared to CNTL. GR100 (Roof with 100% vegetation) is responsible for ~0.5&degC cooling of T2 and a modest reduction in HI and UHI. The magnitude and persistence of the cooling depend strongly on urban density.&nbsp&nbspThe thesis provides a comprehensive assessment of heatwave characteristics, the importance of land use, land cover, and vegetation on heatwave predictability, and effective rooftop-based mitigation strategies to enhance urban thermal resilience under a warming climate.

Keywords: Heatwave, Land surface, urbanization, thermal resilience, future climate, population exposure, India.
